translation: "Shut up," the optician said even louder and walked faster, "Selma seldom finds anything threatening or ugly.
He was right in saying so, but he had unfortunately said more than he should have in response to the voices.
Yet she might find love ugly especially, hissed the voices; there must have been a reason, they suggested, that the truth was hidden for so long.
"That was cowardice," said the optician as he switched his leather bag to his other hip because both its jostling and the voices' constant chatter were starting to hurt.
"Caution it was," retorted the voices.
"Fear can sometimes be a good advisor after all," they added before humming the theme tune of an early evening TV show.
The optician now started to slow down.
Selma's house which normally only took ten minutes to reach suddenly felt like a whole day's journey carrying an immense load of luggage.
That was true.
The dog was the color of slushy snow, a washed-out gray and shaggy like an exclusive Irish Wolfhound without anything else in him.
His body was still small, but his paws were as big as bear claws, and we all knew what that meant.
Selma still stood elevated by the kitchen bench.
She looked at the dog for a long time.
Then she looked at my father as if he were a gift shop.
Farmer Häubel firmly believed that Death would be as polite as he himself had been throughout his life.
He was certain that Death would not snatch life from him, but gently take it from his hand.
He imagined how Death would politely knock, open the door only a crack and ask 'May I? to which Farmer Häubel would naturally respond affirmatively.
'Of course, Farmer Häubel would say, 'do come in, and so Death would enter.
He would stand next to Farmer Häubel's bed and ask, 'Is now a good time for you? I can always come back at a later stage'.

Farmer Häubel would sit up saying No, no, this is just the right moment for me', Let's not postpone it again; who knows when you'll be able to arrange it again, and then Death will sit down on the chair already placed by his head-end.
He will apologize in advance for the coldness of his hands which Bauer Haübel knew wouldn't bother him even slightly before laying them upon farmer Haübel's eyes.
The people in the village were anxious, it was evident, even if most tried to conceal it.
This morning, a few hours after Selma's dream, people moved around the village as though there was black ice underfoot on all paths;
not just outside but within their homes too: black ice in their kitchens and living rooms.
They moved as if their own bodies were completely alien to them, as if all of their joints were inflamed and even the objects they handled could spontaneously combust.
All day long they suspiciously scrutinised their lives and those of everyone else where possible.
Again and again they looked behind them to see if anyone might leap out with murderous intent:
someone who had lost reason, hence had nothing significant left to lose;
also glancing ahead swiftly because someone without reason could also attack from front.
They'd look upward high vigilantly so falling roof tiles, branches or heavy lampshades can't take them by surprise;
avoided every animal because those creatures might turn unexpectedly faster than humansso they thought.
Sidestepped friendly cows which might kick today of all days;
dodged dogs including really old ones that hardly stood up anymore but still possibly would attack at throats this very day.
On such days everything was possible:
being bitten through the throat by an aging dachshund didn't seem more far-fetched than spotting an Okapi suddenly was!
Except for Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, the villagers were mostly not superstitious.

They casually did all the things that one should avoid in superstition: they sat comfortably under wall clocks, though superstition suggests it could lead to death; they slept with their heads towards the door, despite superstition suggesting that it means they would soon be carried out through the same door feet first.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year's which Elsbeth warned was akin to suicide or aiding and abetting a murder in folklore terms without thinking twice.
They didn't get shocked when an owl hooted at night, when a horse sweated profusely in the stable, or when a dog howled at night with its head bowed down.
The train ride lasted fifteen minutes, with no stops in between.

Since our first train ride, we always played the same game: We stood with our backs to the windows by the opposite train doors, Martin closed his eyes, and I looked out from the window of the door behind Martin.
In first grade I described to Martin what I saw during the journey and he tried to remember everything.

He succeeded very well so that in second grade I no longer listed anything and Martin, with his back to the window and eyes closed, was able to recite almost everything that I was seeing through the foggy train window at that moment: "Wire factory," he said exactly as we passed by it.

"What else could it have been," said Selma, and that one could hardly confuse an okapi with another animal.
"Indeed," I said, it might have been a deformed cow, a mis-assembled giraffe, a whim of nature; stripes and rust-red color are all hard to discern at night when everything is very blurred.
"That's nonsense," said Selma, rubbing her forehead.
"It's just plain nonsense, Luise.
She placed a slice of cheese on the bread, folded it and put it in my sandwich box.
"Do you know exactly when you dreamed this?"
Around three o'clock," Selma responded.

She had shot upright after the vision of the okapi had faded away; awakened while still sitting up in bed she stared at her nightgown in which she had just stood on Uhlheck mountain in her dream; then looked over at the clock three o'clock!  "We probably shouldn't take this that seriously," Selma said—yet she sounded like a television detective who doesn't take an anonymous letter seriously.
"What's wrong?"
I asked.
"Nothing," chimed Selma, opening the fridge to take out a packet of sliced cheese and liverwurst, waving them in the air.
"What would you like on your sandwich today?" she cooed.
"Little mouse," she added, and her singing voice and use of 'little mouse' were indeed alarming.
"Cheese please," I said, "what's going on with you?"
"Nothing," chirped Selma, "I just told you.
She spread butter on a slice of bread and because she was still flailing around knocked the cheese packet off the counter with her wrist.
Selma stood still now, looking down at the cheese pack as if it were something precious that had shattered into a thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamed of an okapi three times in her life, and each time someone had died afterwards.
Therefore, we were convinced that dreaming of an okapi and death were definitively connected.
That's how our minds work.
They can ensure that the most far-fetched things belong together within a very short period of time.
Coffee pots and shoelaces for example, or returnable bottles and fir trees.
When I slept downstairs with Selma, she would tell me good-ending stories by the edge of the bed.
When I was younger, she'd take her wrist in my hand after each tale and feel for her pulse, imagining that the entire world moved along to the rhythm of Selma's heartbeat.

I imagined the optician grinding lenses, Martin hoisting a heavy weight, Elsbeth trimming her hedge, how the retail merchant stocked up juice bags; my mother layering pine boughs and my father stamping prescriptions; all doing this precisely in time with Selma's heart rhythm.
This always put me soundly to sleep but now at ten years old, Selma thought I was too old for that.
